title: Java: JUnit Lifecycle and Evidence
summary: Preserve regression meaning with explicit Java resource ownership and assertions.
objectives: Separate Playwright, JUnit and Maven responsibilities
Own contexts and data per test

scenes.title: Own the Java lifecycle
scenes.narration: This episode builds the Java equivalent using Playwright with JUnit. Start by separating the browser library from the test runner. Playwright controls pages and performs its locator assertions; JUnit organizes test execution and records test outcomes. Maven supplies dependencies and launches the configured test process. Those responsibilities do not become identical merely because the TypeScript edition packages them together. Your job is to preserve the three business cases while making resource ownership, assertion choices, and reporting explicit in the Java project.

scenes.title: Inspect the project first
scenes.narration: Open the supplied Maven project and inspect the versions fixed in its project file. Confirm which JSON library it includes, because response parsing examples must match that library. The working hybrid example uses Gson; an example using Jackson needs its own dependency and imports. Also inspect the browser channel configuration before launching. Run Maven's version command to check the selected Java installation. If the project does not compile, treat compiler errors as implementation feedback rather than evidence that the application violated a transfer rule.

scenes.title: Choose ownership boundaries
scenes.narration: For the classroom, begin with sequential tests. A test may own Playwright, the browser, and its context through resource blocks, as in the hybrid example. A larger suite can use JUnit lifecycle methods while keeping one fresh context per case. Whichever structure you choose, draw who closes each object. Avoid a static page shared across tests. Its session, open dialogs, and navigation state can leak between cases even when the test methods look independent in the source file and have different names.
bullets: Test owns Playwright, browser and context
Test creates its own server fixture
Finally: delete the fixture and close browser resources

scenes.title: Create a fresh context
scenes.narration: The excerpt shows the central context boundary inside an existing browser lifecycle. Set the local base address when creating the context, then obtain its page. Authentication happens on this context before protected navigation. Closing the context releases its pages and browser session together. In a lifecycle method, the corresponding cleanup belongs in the matching after method; in a resource block, Java manages closing. Do not mix the two ownership approaches accidentally and leave an object alive because each layer expected another layer to close it.
bullets: Create the page inside its context
scenes.footer: Illustrative Java excerpt · Imports and fixture required

scenes.title: Authenticate with the same identity
scenes.narration: Post the synthetic fixture credentials through the context's request client. Check the response status before reading the transfer page. The displayed request options carry only the business login data; the local test hook key belongs on preparation requests. By keeping those responsibilities separate, your Java test reflects the same authorization model as the other language versions. If login succeeds but navigation appears anonymous, inspect cookie scope and the base address instead of inserting credentials into unrelated requests or bypassing the protected page entirely.
scenes.footer: Illustrative Java excerpt · Imports and fixture required

scenes.title: Use Java locator assertions
scenes.narration: After selecting the source and beneficiary, fill the amount field and submit through the accessible button. Use Playwright's assertion import for the visible balance, because it provides locator-aware waiting. JUnit's ordinary equality assertion remains appropriate for values you already obtained from an API response. These assertions serve different observations, so inspect the imports when AI generates a test. A method named assertThat from another library may have entirely different behavior even if the surrounding Java code looks familiar and the editor offers an automatic import.
scenes.footer: Illustrative Java excerpt · Imports and fixture required

scenes.title: Inspect the integer account balance
scenes.narration: Fetch the source account through the same context and verify the successful response before parsing its body. The excerpt uses Gson, matching the supplied hybrid Java project. Compare the balance in minor units and preserve the source identifier in your report. Next, read the canonical transfer collection and check its count and complete business fields. Parsing a number is not enough if the query selected the wrong account. This is why fixture identifiers remain visible through the action and every following assertion.
scenes.footer: Illustrative Java excerpt · Imports and fixture required

scenes.title: Implement rejection and replay
scenes.narration: Create separate fixtures for the rejection and replay tests. For rejection, verify the business error, unchanged balance, and empty transfer list. For replay, send the same request body and key twice, verify the creation and replay response statuses, and compare their identifiers. Keep the final balance and count assertions even when both identifiers match. Java's request option objects do not create idempotency by themselves; the server contract interprets the key. Make that relationship explicit in the test name and review the generated request construction carefully.

scenes.title: Record a Java trace
scenes.narration: Start tracing before the browser actions you want to diagnose, then stop and save it before closing the context. The excerpt shows the lifecycle calls. Your fixture or JUnit extension decides when to retain the artifact and how to name it per test. Keep the JUnit outcome alongside the trace, because the library trace is not a replacement for the runner's assertion report. Verify this arrangement using an actual failure rather than assuming a configured filename guarantees a useful diagnostic artifact.
scenes.footer: Illustrative Java excerpt · Imports and fixture required

scenes.title: Avoid unsafe parallel sharing
scenes.narration: Only add parallel execution after the sequential suite is reproducible. Playwright Java objects should remain on their owning thread unless you implement the required synchronization. Give each parallel execution its own Playwright instance and keep calls on that thread. This is separate from data isolation: independent browser objects can still collide when they mutate one shared account. Review both the thread ownership and fixture identifiers before increasing concurrency, and keep failures attributable to one test attempt rather than a mixture of overlapping sessions.

scenes.title: Read the actual runner result
scenes.narration: Run the selected Maven test and inspect its Surefire reports. A successful compilation is only the preparation stage; the result must show that the intended test method actually executed. Confirm the number of tests and inspect failures or skipped cases. If a browser or terminal dependency is unavailable, keep that limitation in the report. For hybrid work later, a Java test may invoke the Python adapter as a bounded subprocess, but Java still owns the final assertion about the returned correlation and business values.
scenes.code:
mvn -Dtest=HybridTransferTest test
# Inspect target/surefire-reports after the run.

scenes.title: Compare meaning across languages
scenes.narration: Place the Java, Python, and TypeScript evidence matrices beside each other. Each should describe the same starting balance, transfer amount, rejection behavior, and single-effect replay. The lifecycle, configuration, and artifact commands differ; the business promise does not. Explain why you used a locator assertion for the browser and a value assertion for parsed JSON. Then point to cleanup and the actual result files. The skill is adapting test architecture to a language without quietly weakening what the regression is supposed to prove.
